## The one-line version

`lint:no-raw-setinterval` sat **red on staging for ~20 hours** and nothing told anyone.
Meanwhile `lint:guard-reachability` scored it **ENFORCED** — and *that score was correct*.
A blocking path genuinely does run it. It just never runs it **before the code it polices is
promoted**.

> **The question to ask of any guard is not "is it reachable?" but "does it run before the
> thing it polices ships?"** Those are different properties, and only the second one is
> enforcement.

## How a guard becomes reachable-but-useless

`lint:no-raw-setinterval` had exactly one blocking invocation
(`.github/workflows/test.yml:265`). That workflow's triggers:

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
```

`push` and `pull_request` look like pre-merge gates. **Here they are inert.** Every commit
git-sync produces carries a literal `[skip ci]`, and `main` only ever fast-forwards from a
staging commit — so every commit `main` advances to carries it too. GitHub Actions honors
`[skip ci]` for both events, so **neither trigger has fired on a real `main` advance since
the staging→main model landed.**

`workflow_dispatch` is a distinct trigger type that `[skip ci]` does *not* filter, and
green-checkpoint fires it explicitly **right after** each fast-forward of `main`. So the
guard does run — on a blocking path — **immediately after promotion.** It can tell you that
what you already shipped was bad.

That is why a reachability scorer says ENFORCED and is not lying. Reachability asks *does
any blocking path invoke this?* The answer was yes. It is simply the wrong question.

**The fix** was to give the guard a green-checkpoint leg, so it runs against the candidate
*before* the fast-forward rather than after it:

```ts
// apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts
const lintTimerClassCheck        = haltedBy ? null : checkNpmScript(treeDir, 'lint:timer-classification');
const lintNoRawSetintervalCheck  = haltedBy ? null : checkNpmScript(treeDir, 'lint:no-raw-setinterval');
```

**Generalisation:** on this repo, a lint that exists only in `.github/workflows/` is
*post-hoc*, not gating. If you want a guard to block, it needs a green-checkpoint leg. Ask
where your guard runs before you trust it to protect anything.

## Trap 2 — verifying "is my guard live?" against the wrong object

While writing this page I formed a reasonable hypothesis: the new legs landed on staging at
01:55 and 04:39, but `main` last advanced at 00:56 — so surely the legs are not executing
yet? The check seemed obvious:

```bash
git show origin/main:apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts | grep -c lintNoRawSetintervalCheck   # 0
grep -c lintNoRawSetintervalCheck ../papercup-release/apps/.../green-checkpoint.ts                       # 0
```

Two independent sources, both zero. Clean, corroborated, and **wrong** — because
`green-checkpoint.ts` **does not run from `main` or the release checkout at all.** It is a
detached CLI spawned per run with `--working-directory` pinned to the **staging integration
tree**, executed by `papercup-bg-host.service`. A `:3070` deploy never changes what it runs;
the next invocation picks up the edit directly.

Both greps were accurate measurements **of an object that does not execute this code.** The
authoritative answer is one call:

```
dev:pipeline_position { path: "apps/operator/lib/release/green-checkpoint.ts" }
```

which replies in as many words: *"runs in bg-host — NOT carried by the staging→main→:3070
deploy … your edit is already what the NEXT invocation runs."*

**The shape to recognise:** a *correct* measurement of the wrong object is far more
dangerous than a failed one, because corroboration feels like confirmation. Two greps
agreeing proved only that they shared my false premise. Before concluding "my change is not
live", establish **which process, from which tree,** actually executes it — never infer it
from the branch a file happens to sit on.

## Trap 3 — a citation is not evidence

`check-timer-classification.mjs` cited `client-timer-classification.test.ts` **twice** as
what keeps the two-guard handoff airtight, and `check-no-raw-setinterval.mjs` called that
handoff "an INVARIANT, asserted by" the same file.

`git log --all` on that path was **empty**. The file had never been committed. The client
scan shipped with **zero tests** while its own header asserted the opposite — in a confident,
specific, load-bearing sentence.

It exists now (144 lines, 16 assertions, including the three handoff cases that prove no file
falls between the two guards). It exists because someone checked the citation.

**Rule:** a comment asserting that a test guarantees a property is a *claim*, not the
property. `git log` the cited path. This is the same family as the repo's documented case of
a doc crediting a fix to a sibling field that never received it — and note that the more
authoritative the prose sounds, the less likely anyone is to check it.

> ⚠ **Corollary, learned on this very page:** an inherited finding can be *true when written
> and false when you read it*. The checkpoint handing me this work stated the test was "never
> committed" — accurate at the time, already fixed by the time I inherited it. Had I
> transcribed it, I would have published a falsehood with a citation attached. Re-run the
> evidence; never republish a finding you have not re-measured.

## Trap 4 — encoding a property as comment PLACEMENT

`no-raw-setinterval`'s browser/client exemption used to be expressed by **which comment
heading an entry sat under**. Two of the entries already sat under the "Separate processes"
heading with their own inline `// browser ...` note — so any check that read the section
header would have mis-partitioned them **while looking perfectly rigorous.**

The fix makes membership a named, exported set:

```js
export const BROWSER_CLIENT_ALLOWLIST = new Set([ /* ... */ ]);
export const SEPARATE_PROCESS_ALLOWLIST = new Set([ /* ... */ ]);
```

**Anchor a property to a declaration, never to how a comment happens to be spelled.** This is
the same correction CLAUDE.md records three times over for population measurements that
matched a *spelling* instead of the *property* — each caught only after it had produced a
confident wrong count.

## The through-line

All four traps share one shape: **the artifact that tells you a guard is sound is itself
unverified.** A reachability score, a header citation, a comment heading, a branch's
contents — each is a *representation* of enforcement, and each can be true, well-formed, and
disconnected from what actually executes.

When you need to know whether a guard protects you, do not read what the guard says about
itself. Establish (1) **where** it runs, (2) **when** it runs relative to promotion, and
(3) **that its stated evidence exists.**
